The Double is Dostoevsky's second published work from 1846, presenting Yakov Petrovich Golyadkin, a meek copying clerk whose fragile sanity unravels when an exact double of himself appears. The doppelgänger is everything Golyadkin desires and fears: confident, socially ascendant, ruthlessly selfish. This makes the novella a hallucinatory descent into paranoia and the fracture of identity. Golyadkin is a petty bureaucrat tormented by social anxiety and wounded pride, desperate to advance and be accepted in society. His double embodies the ruthless will he cannot access. The double initially appears as his brother but gradually supplants him in society, at work, and even in claiming his identity. Golyadkin cannot convince anyone that the double is not himself. The narrative voice becomes increasingly unreliable as Golyadkin's grasp on reality weakens. Readers cannot be certain whether the double is external or a projection of disintegrating consciousness. The novella blends the grotesque realism of Poor Folk with psychological distortion. It anticipates modernist interior monologue and the exploration of mental breakdown. Dostoevsky was influenced by E.T.A. Hoffmann's romanticism and the literary tradition of doppelgängers, yet his version is uniquely social and political. The double represents the triumph of social conformity and competitive will. Published in Notes of the Fatherland, early critics found it confusing. Its reputation grew as psychological realism became a central literary concern. Today it stands as an experimental novella establishing Dostoevsky's lifelong interest in fractured consciousness and the unstable nature of identity itself.
